{"needed":true,"prompt":"Scope: Frontend-only implementation to record, expose and handle an in-session “undo” (restore) for items that were successfully deleted during this browser session. Uses the provided backend endpoint POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore (no body). Do not add new backend calls or assume other backend endpoints beyond the restore endpoint and the fact that a delete operation elsewhere in the app already reports success to the frontend.

Assumptions you must NOT make: do not assume item shape fields beyond that the restore endpoint returns an ItemPublic object with deleted_at=null on success; do not assume any list endpoint paths, sorting rules, page sizes, or persistent storage for undo entries. Keep undo state in-memory only (cleared on page refresh) as required.

Implementation steps:

1) In-memory session store
- Add an in-memory store to record ids of items that were successfully deleted in this session. Example structure: a Set deletedSessionIds and an optional map deletedUndoMetadata keyed by id (to store label/title for UX or an undo timer handle). This must be in memory (module-level variable, React Context, or equivalent) and not persisted to localStorage or cookies.

2) When an item deletion completes successfully elsewhere in the app
- After receiving a successful delete response (this code path already exists in the app), do the following:
  a) Add the item id to deletedSessionIds and store any needed metadata (display name/title) in deletedUndoMetadata.
  b) Show a short-lived undo affordance to the user: a snackbar/toast or inline temporary banner with an explicit “Undo” button for that id. Typical lifetime: ~5–10 seconds. Also allow the user to click Undo immediately (no need to wait for timer). The undo affordance must be session-only and disappear on page refresh.

3) Undo UI and interaction options (pick one or both)
- Snackbar/Toast: Show message like “Item "<title>" deleted” with a clickable Undo button.
- Inline row-level undo: if the list view keeps a placeholder where the deleted item was, show an “Undo” link until the snackbar expires.
- Important: don’t create a new “recycle bin” list interface; keep undo transient and session-scoped.

4) Restore request (Undo handler)
- When the user clicks Undo for id:
  a) Send an HTTP POST request to /api/v1/items/{id}/restore with method POST and no body. Include whatever auth headers/cookies your app uses (e.g., Authorization: Bearer <token> or cookies) — reuse existing auth logic. Example fetch pseudocode:
     fetch(`/api/v1/items/${id}/restore`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': 'Bearer <token>' } })
  b) On success (HTTP 200): the server returns an ItemPublic object and deleted_at must be null. Use that returned object to update client state (see step 5). Remove id from deletedSessionIds and clear its undo UI.
  c) Error handling: handle the following status codes explicitly and map them to user-facing messages:
     - 409: detail="Item is not deleted" — show a message like “Item is not deleted; cannot restore.” Remove id from deletedSessionIds and clear the undo UI because undo is no longer valid.
     - 404: show “Item no longer exists (404).” Remove id from deletedSessionIds and clear undo UI.
     - 403: show “You do not have permission to restore this item.” Remove id from deletedSessionIds and clear undo UI.
     - Other errors (5xx or network): show appropriate error toast and keep the undo affordance removed (recommended) or re-enable it based on your UX choice. Prefer removing the undo entry because the server state is authoritative.
  d) Do not retry automatically; surface the error to the user and log for diagnostics.

5) Integrating restored item into the UI and counts
- Use the ItemPublic returned by the restore response as the canonical source to re-add/update the UI. Two safe options (choose what fits your app):
  Option A (preferred if you want exact server state and have an existing list fetch utility):
    - If your app has an existing list refresh function (re-fetch current page), call that function to obtain the current canonical list and counts (preferred for correctness across pagination, sorting and server-side filters).
    - If you call the list refresh, ensure the UI count/total is updated by the refreshed response.
  Option B (if you cannot or prefer not to re-fetch):
    - Insert the returned ItemPublic object directly into client-side list state and increment the total count variable by +1.
    - Placement: If you know the client-side sort key, compute the correct insertion index. If you do not know or don’t want to compute it, insert the item at the top of the current list (or at a chosen default position) so it is visible. Document this behavior for product/QA because it may not match server sort order.
- After reinserting, re-render list and ensure any UI that shows the total count is incremented.
- If your UI uses pagination and the current page was full, apply your app’s existing policy (e.g., drop the last row of the page to keep page size, or refresh the page contents). Prefer re-fetch for correctness.

6) Concurrency and race conditions
- If multiple undo requests are issued or if the server reports that the item is already restored/changed, handle 409/404/403 as in step 4b and remove the session undo entry.
- If the user clicks Undo but the network is slow, disable the Undo button while the request is in flight to avoid duplicate requests.

7) Telemetry and logging
- Log restore successes and failures to your existing client-side telemetry with item id and status code to help backend debugging. Do not log sensitive user tokens.

8) UX edge-cases and QA checklist
- Verify that after successful restore: the item appears in the list and the total count increments.
- Verify 409 response leads to a clear message and that undo entry disappears.
- Verify 404 and 403 handling as described.
- Verify undo entries do not persist after page reload (in-memory only).
- Verify that repeated delete -> undo cycles behave deterministically.

9) Example pseudo-code (framework-agnostic) for Undo handler
- On delete success:
    deletedSessionIds.add(id)
    deletedUndoMetadata[id] = { title: itemTitle }
    showSnackbar({ message: `Deleted ${itemTitle}`, action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: () => undoRestore(id) } })
- undoRestore(id):
    disableUndoButton(id)
    resp = await fetch(`/api/v1/items/${id}/restore`, { method: 'POST', headers: authHeaders })
    if resp.status === 200:
       restoredItem = await resp.json()
       if restoredItem.deleted_at !== null:
          showError('Server returned item still deleted; contact support')
       else:
          deletedSessionIds.delete(id)
          delete deletedUndoMetadata[id]
          closeSnackbarFor(id)
          // update list and count
          if (hasListRefreshFunction) callListRefresh()
          else insertRestoredItemIntoList(restoredItem) and totalCount += 1
          showToast('Item restored')
    else if resp.status === 409:
       deletedSessionIds.delete(id); delete deletedUndoMetadata[id]; closeSnackbarFor(id)
       showError('Item is not deleted')
    else if resp.status === 404:
       deletedSessionIds.delete(id); delete deletedUndoMetadata[id]; closeSnackbarFor(id)
       showError('Item not found (404)')
    else if resp.status === 403:
       deletedSessionIds.delete(id); delete deletedUndoMetadata[id]; closeSnackbarFor(id)
       showError('Permission denied (403)')
    else:
       showError('Restore failed; please try again')
       // optionally re-enable undo, but prefer removing it to avoid stale state

Deliverables for engineers implementing this:
- Add an in-memory deletedSessionIds store and metadata map.
- Wire delete-success path to add ids to the store and display undo UI.
- Implement undo handler that calls POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore and handles 200/409/404/403 explicitly.
- On 200, use the returned ItemPublic to reintegrate the restored item into the visible list and increment counts (or re-fetch current list if available).
- Ensure all undo UIs are removed on success or the specified error cases. Keep undo entries session-only and non-persistent.

Notes: Follow the exact API contract given: POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore (no body). Expect 200 with ItemPublic and deleted_at=null on success; expect 409 with detail="Item is not deleted" when trying to restore a non-deleted item; expect 404 for missing item and 403 for permission errors. Do not invent additional endpoints or persistence for undo entries."}

**Implementing undo functionality**

I'm thinking about how to provide an undo UI. I should show a toast or snackbar with an Undo button for the deleted item and also display a "Recently deleted" banner in the list. Clicking Undo would trigger a call to the POST restore endpoint, and if successful, I'd need to update the list and count. Since the undo entries won't survive a page refresh, I should rely on in-memory storage. Additionally, I need to handle pagination carefully to ensure the restored item displays correctly.**Considering safe restoration approaches**

I’m thinking about two safe methods to restore items: the optimistic approach, where I add the item returned from the server directly to the in-memory list and increment the count, versus the conservative approach, which involves calling the current list API to get the canonical state. However, I need to avoid guessing unresolved contracts, so instead, I should use the ItemPublic from the restore response and manage successfully deleted IDs for undo functionality. That way, I’ll ensure a smooth user experience!**Handling item restoration**

When the restoration is successful, the backend will return an ItemPublic. I need to ensure that the deleted_at field is null, remove the ID from sessionDeletedIds, and update the UI by inserting the returned item into the list and incrementing the total count.

If the list involves client-side filtering or pagination, I have to be cautious about where to place the restored item. It's better to provide options, like re-fetching the whole list if that's supported, or inserting the item at the top if not. However, I must avoid making assumptions about sorting unless I know the sorting key.**Defining the project scope**

I’m deciding to focus on React for my project scope based on the developer's guidance to generate frontend implementation instructions. I want to keep things somewhat framework-agnostic but will provide example code patterns in pseudocode or JavaScript using Fetch and typical UI patterns. The instructions will be structured in JSON format with a prompt string for clear steps. This will include implementing session-only undo for deletes, managing in-memory sessionDeletedIds, and showing a snackbar or toast for undo actions. When the Undo button is pressed, I’ll call the appropriate REST API for restoration.**Implementing response handling**

When I receive a response with a status of 200, I need to validate that the returned item has deleted_at set to null, remove its ID from sessionDeletedIds, and update the client list by inserting the item and incrementing the counts. If the response is a 409, I should indicate that the item is not deleted, remove the ID, and for a 404, show that the item is not found. For a 403, since the user lacks permission, I should remove the ID too.

If there are errors, I’ll remove the undo entry and display the corresponding error messages. Also, when updating the list, I should consider whether it’s in-memory and handle pagination safely. If re-fetching is supported, I can recommend that as the safest route. Lastly, I’ll prepare the content with clear steps and example code in pseudocode or JavaScript, keeping the format concise!
